title: Counting steps
summary: Measure an algorithm by how many steps it takes, not by how many seconds.

steps.title: Steps, not seconds
body: A stopwatch tells you how fast code ran on *your* machine today. Computer scientists ask a sturdier question: **how many basic steps does it take, as the input grows?**
A basic step is anything that takes a fixed amount of work: an addition, a comparison, reading `a[i]`.
Press play below and watch `steps` climb once per item. Four items, four trips round the loop. A million items would mean a million trips.
> **Tip:** Use the step buttons to move one line at a time. Watch the variables panel: `total` and `steps` change on every pass.

steps.explain: The loop body runs once per item: four items, four steps. The work grows in a straight line with the input.

steps.prompt: A loop does one step per item. You make the input **ten times** bigger. Roughly how many steps does it take now?
steps.explain: One step per item means steps grow exactly as fast as the input: ten times the items, ten times the steps.

steps.title: Loops inside loops
body: Put a loop inside a loop and the inner body runs once for **every pair** `(i, j)`. With `n` items that is `n × n` steps.
Watch the counter below. With `n = 3` the inner line runs 3 times for `i = 0`, 3 times for `i = 1`, 3 times for `i = 2`: nine in total.
Double `n` to 6 and it runs 36 times: **four** times as many. That is why nested loops over big data feel slow so suddenly.

steps.prompt: The inner loop now starts at `i + 1`, so each **pair** is counted once. What does this print?
code: for (var j = i + 1; j < n; j++)
steps.explain: For `i = 0` the inner loop runs 4 times, then 3, 2, 1, 0. That is 4 + 3 + 2 + 1 = 10, which is `n × (n - 1) / 2`. Still roughly half of `n²`, so it grows the same way.
hints: Count the inner runs for each `i`: 4 when `i` is 0, then one fewer each time.

steps.prompt: Each snippet runs with `n = 10`. Match it to how many times `work++` runs.
pairs: `for (i = 0; i < n; i++) for (j = 0; j < n; j++) work++;`
steps.explain: A single loop scales with `n`, two nested loops with `n × n`. Doing two steps per pass doubles the count but it still grows in a straight line.

steps.prompt: Complete the loops so `pairs` counts every pair `(i, j)` with `i < j` exactly once.
steps.explain: Starting `j` at `i + 1` skips the pair of an item with itself and never counts `(1, 0)` after `(0, 1)`.

steps.title: Count equal pairs
prompt: Write `int CountEqualPairs(int[] a)`: how many pairs of positions `i < j` hold the same value.
Use two nested loops, like the pair counter above.
starter: // compare every i with every j > i
solution: for (var j = i + 1; j < a.Length; j++)
template: Dojo.Eq("an empty array has none", 0, CountEqualPairs(new int[0]));
hints: Outer loop over `i` from 0, inner loop over `j` from `i + 1`.
